Empirical Research Plan  
“Children and the Gender Gap: Evidence from Danish Administrative Data”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Event–study difference-in-differences (DiD).

• Why event–study?  
  – Birth of the first child is a clearly dated, one-off shock.  
  – Annual panels allow us to trace dynamics up to ≥10 years before and after.  

• Why DiD?  
  – We compare the same individual before vs. after the event (first difference) and mothers vs. fathers (second difference).  
  – Fathers serve as a contemporaneous control for aggregate shocks (business cycle, tax reforms, etc.).

Formally,

Y_it = Σ_{k≠–1} β_k · Post_k,it × Female_i  + γ_i + δ_t + ε_it,  
where k indexes event time (years from birth), γ_i are individual FEs, and δ_t
year FEs.

The β_k trace the “child penalty” to mothers relative to fathers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treated = year t ≥ 0 for women whose first child arrives in year 0.  
• Control = ( i ) the same women during t<0; ( ii ) men who become fathers in year 0 during all t.

Treatment timing / event date  
• Event date = calendar year of first childbirth recorded in the Civil Register.  
• Sample restricted to first births 1985–2010 to guarantee ≥5 yrs of pre- and post-data.

Control group  
1. Primary: Biological fathers of the same cohort of first births.  
2. Secondary robustness: Women and men who remain childless through age 45, assigned a placebo event date drawn from the fertility-timing distribution.

No running variable; not an RDD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: Absent childbirth, mothers-to-be and fathers-to-be would have followed the same earnings trajectory.  
• Plausibility: Both are drawn from the same couples’ pool; Denmark’s labor-market gender gap is relatively small pre-child.  
• Test: Inspect coefficients β_k for k<0; they should be statistically and economically flat.

A2. No differential anticipation effects that violate parallelism.  
• Plausibility: Pregnancy is largely known only within a year prior, and we include k=–2,…,–5 to check for early divergences.

A3. Stable composition: No selective attrition that differs by gender after birth (e.g., migration, death).  
• Plausibility: Out-migration and mortality at childbearing ages are very low in Denmark; still testable.

A4. SUTVA / no spillovers: One parent’s labor-supply response does not mechanically bias the other’s response in the DiD because we difference across gender.  
• Plausibility: Some intra-household spillovers exist, but they are the object of interest (they do not contaminate β_k).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Pre-trend differences or differential fertility timing by career prospects.  
• Mitigation:  
  – Plot event-study for t = –10,…,–1; formally test joint significance.  
  – Add couple fixed effects where feasible (compare mother to her partner).  
  – Control for age at birth, education, pre-birth earnings decile interacted with time.

Threat 2: Policy changes (parental-leave reforms, tax reforms) occurring near certain birth cohorts.  
• Mitigation:  
  – Include cohort×year FE blocks or control for policy dummies.  
  – Estimate separately for sub-periods with stable legislation.

Threat 3: Endogenous labor-market shocks tied to pregnancy (e.g., employer laying off pregnant women).  
• Mitigation:  
  – Use firm×year FE in robustness checks to difference out common firm shocks.  
  – Use alternative outcomes (hours worked, employment indicator) to see if earnings results are driven by job loss vs. hours.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE estimators
library(ggplot2)      # plotting
library(broom)        # tidy outputs

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data  (assume earnings_data.csv in working dir)
# -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("earnings_data.csv")   # one row per person-year

# key vars expected in file:
# id, year, earnings, employment, birth_year_child1, gender (0=male,1=female),
# age, educ, firm_id (optional)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct event-time dummies
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# keep individuals who ever have a child in 1985-2010
dt <- dt[!is.na(birth_year_child1) & birth_year_child1 %between% c(1985,2010)]

# Event time
dt[, event_time := year - birth_year_child1]

# trim window
dt <- dt[event_time >= -10 & event_time <= 10]

# Create event-time factors excluding -1 (baseline)
for(k in c(-10:-2,0:10)){
  dt[, paste0("ev",sprintf("%+d",k)) := as.integer(event_time==k)]
}

# control vars
dt[, female := as.integer(gender==1)]
dt[, age_sq := age^2]

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Event-Study Regression
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# formula: earnings ~ Σ ev_k * female + FE(i) + FE(year)
ev_terms <- paste0("ev",sprintf("%+d",c(-10:-2,0:10)),":female", collapse=" + ")
fml <- as.formula(paste("log(earnings+1) ~", ev_terms, 
                        "+ age + age_sq | id + year"))

est <- feols(fml, data=dt, se="cluster[id]")

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Plot coefficients
# -----------------------------------------------------------
coefs <- broom::tidy(est)[grepl("ev", term)]
coefs$event_time <- as.integer(sub("ev([+-]?[0-9]+):female","\\1",coefs$term))

ggplot(coefs, aes(event_time, estimate)) + 
  geom_point() + geom_line() + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=estimate-1.96*std.error,
                    ymax=estimate+1.96*std.error)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x="Years relative to first birth", y="Log-earnings gap (women-men)")

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Couple Fixed Effects
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Need partner_id and restrict to couples observed together
# assuming partner_id variable exists
couple_dt <- dt[!is.na(partner_id)]
est_couple <- feols(fml, data=couple_dt, cluster="partner_id")

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Save results
# -----------------------------------------------------------
etable(est, est_couple, file="child_penalty_results.txt")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory and prior empirical evidence suggest:

• Immediate effect: In year 0–1, mothers’ earnings fall sharply (~30 %).  
• Medium- to long-run (year 10): Persistent gap of ~20 % relative to fathers, with only partial convergence.  
• Fathers experience essentially zero or even slightly positive effects on earnings (overtime, promotions).

Hence β_k<0 for k≥0, with β_5 ≈ –0.25 log-points and β_10 ≈ –0.20.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-Study DiD)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends hold? ................. 0.8  
C2: No simultaneous confounders? .............. 0.7  
C3: No composition changes / attrition? ....... 0.9  
C4: Correct functional form & bandwidth? ...... 0.8  
C5: Correct inference (cluster, serial corr.) . 1.0  

Average score: 0.84 → method judged reasonably valid, but continued scrutiny of C1–C2 is essential.
